analysis.one_liner: Extends do-not-call protections to all phone lines and makes illegal robocallers easier to sue.
analysis.headline: The bill has sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee since its April 2026 introduction, with two cosponsors and no hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, do-not-call protections apply only to residential phone lines, and a person can generally sue over unwanted robocalls only after two calls from the same company within a year, with damages of up to $500 per violation. This bill extends those protections to every phone subscriber, including cell phones, lets a single unwanted call trigger a lawsuit, makes the $500-per-violation penalty mandatory rather than an 'up to' ceiling, and broadens the definition of the auto-dialing equipment the rules apply to. It would also require the FCC to update its rules within 270 days of enactment.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone who gets unwanted robocalls, telemarketing calls, or spam texts, which today means nearly everyone with a phone, including people whose cell lines fall outside the current do-not-call rules. People who could now sue after a single violating call, with a guaranteed $500 penalty per call, would have a real financial lever against companies that ignore the rules.

how_it_helps.text: Strikes the word 'residential' from the do-not-call provisions of the Communications Act, so the rules cover all telephone subscribers rather than only residential lines [S2].
Changes the private right of action so a single call in violation of the do-not-call rules can support a lawsuit, replacing the current two-calls-in-12-months threshold [S2].
Removes the words 'up to' from the penalty provision, making the statutory penalty mandatory rather than a discretionary ceiling of up to $500 per violation [S2].

Broadens the definition of 'automatic telephone dialing system' to include equipment that dials from a stored list of telephone numbers, closing an avenue robocallers use to argue they are not covered [S2].
Requires the FCC to revise its regulations within 270 days of enactment to implement the expanded protections [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Telemarketers, robocall operations, debt collectors, and other businesses that reach people by automated phone calls would face stricter rules and a much greater risk of lawsuits with guaranteed $500 penalties per call. Companies that call customers with legitimate reminders, such as appointment or payment notices, would also have less margin for error before becoming liable.

drawbacks.text: Letting a single unwanted call trigger a lawsuit with a mandatory penalty would expose legitimate businesses, such as pharmacies, banks, or doctors' offices making automated appointment or payment reminders, to litigation costs over isolated mistakes [S2].

Making the $500-per-violation penalty mandatory rather than an 'up to' ceiling removes judicial discretion to reduce damages in low-harm cases, which increases the cost of defending routine calls [S2].
A broader definition of auto-dialing equipment could sweep in ordinary reminder systems and messaging software, pushing some legitimate communications channels to avoid calling entirely [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to consumers is real: the current rules leave cell phones underprotected and make it easy for callers to violate them repeatedly with little consequence. The cost is that the one-call, mandatory-penalty design is aggressive and could create liability for low-harm legitimate calls. A well-designed version would target predatory robocalling while giving good-faith callers some margin; as written, it leans heavily toward maximum enforcement.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in April 2026 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, where it has received no further action while Congress remains in session [S4].

narrative.text: Rep. Jan Schakowsky introduced the bill on April 15, 2026, for herself and Rep. Mullin [S2].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day, and the action history shows no hearing, markup, floor vote, or other action since [S4].
The bill has two cosponsors, both Democrats [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has changed position: the bill has simply not moved. Telemarketers, robocall operations, and other automated callers are better off with the status quo, since they continue operating under the weaker existing rules while the bill sits untouched in committee.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Automated callers; the bill has not moved

for.name: Jan Schakowsky
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill expanding do-not-call coverage and robocall penalties [S2].

for.name: Mullin
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor of the bill [S2].

for.name: Two House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's only cosponsors [S3].

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors and cosponsors are Democrats and no member has publicly opposed the bill, but it has not advanced far enough for any vote to reveal where members actually stand.

industries.note: The bill extends do-not-call coverage to all phone subscribers, lets one violating call trigger a lawsuit, and makes the $500-per-call penalty mandatory. Its business model depends on calling large numbers of consumers who have not invited the contact [S2].
Collectors rely heavily on automated dialing of consumer cell phones; broader auto-dialer definitions and a one-call right of action would substantially raise their litigation exposure [S2].

industries.industry: Businesses using automated reminders (healthcare, banking, retail)
industries.note: These firms call their own customers for appointments and account matters and do not oppose the rules on principle, but the bill's one-call lawsuit trigger and mandatory penalty would apply to their legitimate calls as well, giving them reason to worry about isolated errors [S2].

analysis.trajectory: Most House bills never get a hearing or vote, and this one has drawn only two cosponsors in months of sitting on the Energy and Commerce Committee's plate. Without a chairman decision to schedule a markup or bipartisan support, the realistic path is that it dies at the end of the 119th Congress without a floor vote.
